on balance: gives your opinion after weighing all the facts, good and bad
typical: neutral to formal, at the start of a sentence or between commas. NOT for: a quick first impression.
On balance, the second offer seems better.
It was, on balance, a good year for the company.
On balance, we think it's better to wait.
on the contrary: adds that the opposite of a negative statement is true
typical: after your own negative statement, e.g. It isn't X; on the contrary, it is Y. NOT for: a mild contrast between two different things (use 'by contrast').
The new system isn't slower; on the contrary, it's twice as fast.
Moving abroad wasn't a mistake. On the contrary, it was the best decision of my life.
He isn't lazy; on the contrary, he works harder than anyone.
strongly disagrees with what someone else has said or suggested
typical: spoken, at the start of a reply, also 'quite the contrary'. NOT for: agreeing with someone.
'Sorry, I'm probably boring you.' 'On the contrary, I find it fascinating.'
'Was the film a disaster?' 'Quite the contrary, it was brilliant.'
'You must hate living here.' 'On the contrary, I love it.'
on the one hand: introduces the first of two points that you want to weigh against each other
typical: in discussions and essays, followed later by 'on the other hand'; always 'on the one hand', not 'on one hand'. NOT for: a single point with nothing to compare it to.
On the one hand, working from home saves time; on the other hand, it can feel lonely.
On the one hand, I'd love to live abroad. On the other hand, I'd miss my family.
On the one hand, the course is expensive; however, it will help my career.
on the other hand: gives another fact or opinion that should be considered together with the one you have just given
typical: after 'on the one hand', after 'but', or at the start of a new sentence. NOT for: correcting a wrong idea (use 'on the contrary').
The job pays well. On the other hand, the hours are very long.
I'd like a bigger flat. On the other hand, I don't want a higher rent.
Living in the city is exciting; on the other hand, it is noisy and expensive.
open up: begin to talk openly about your feelings
typical: open up (to sb/about sth). NOT for: opening a door or box.
He finally opened up to me about his fears.
It takes time for some children to open up.
start a business or open a shop for customers
typical: open up a shop/an office; the café opens up at seven. NOT for: closing it.
They plan to open up a bakery in the old station.
The café opens up at seven.
typical: open up chances/possibilities, open sth up. NOT for: closing options.
The new law will open up new markets.
A degree can open up many career options.
opt out: choose not to take part in something
typical: opt out (of sth), e.g. opt out of the plan. NOT for: choosing to join (use opt in).
Employees can opt out of the pension scheme.
Three schools opted out of the programme.
or: alternative
shows a choice between two or more possibilities
typical: questions and lists, e.g. tea or coffee, walk or bus. NOT for: adding things together (use 'and').
Do you want to walk or take the bus?
You can pay by card or in cash.
Is the meeting on Monday or on Tuesday?
vague example
says that other similar things could also be named
typical: spoken, e.g. or something, or anything. NOT for: exact information or formal writing.
Shall we watch a film or something?
He didn't even smile or anything.
I think she works as a nurse or something.
correction
corrects what you just said or makes it more exact
typical: or rather, or at least, or maybe. NOT for: offering a real choice.
We met in May, or rather at the end of April.
It took an hour, or at least it felt like one.
She's thirty, or maybe thirty-one; I never remember.
warning
warns that something bad will happen if the first thing is not done
typical: after a command, also with 'or else'. NOT for: a neutral choice between two options.
Lock the door or someone might walk in.
Study tonight or you'll regret it tomorrow.
Be on time, or else we'll leave without you.
otherwise: says what bad thing will happen if the first thing is not done
typical: after an instruction or a necessary action, e.g. Book early, otherwise... NOT for: a neutral choice between two options (use 'or').
Check your bag, otherwise you might leave something behind.
Book early, otherwise there won't be any seats.
Take notes, otherwise you'll forget everything.
says what would have happened if the first thing had not happened
typical: after a fact about the past, e.g. I took a map. Otherwise, I would have... NOT for: warnings about the future.
I took a map. Otherwise, I would have got lost in the old town.
She called a taxi. Otherwise, she would have missed her flight.
Luckily, the doctor came quickly; otherwise, it could have been serious.
overall: gives a general judgement about the whole situation after looking at the details
typical: at the start of a sentence or after 'but', neutral. NOT for: a judgement based on one detail only.
Overall, I enjoyed the course, although the exams were stressful.
The service was slow at times, but overall it was good.
says that something is true when everything is counted or included together
typical: at the end of a clause with numbers, positions or amounts. NOT for: giving a general opinion at the start of a sentence.
He finished second overall in the tournament.
The repairs will cost about two thousand euros overall.
We spent four days on the project overall.
own up: admit that you did something wrong
typical: own up (to sth/to doing sth). NOT for: blaming someone else.
Nobody owned up to breaking the window.
He owned up and said sorry.
